tldr: By automatically generating physically viable whole-body trajectories from human interaction data and distilling a privileged teacher into a student policy relying purely on onboard sensors, ViLoMan achieves a unified control policy that completes door-closing tasks without external commands or reference motions.
hero_caption: Snapshots of ViLoMan executing door-closing tasks using a single policy. Even with large variations in the robot's initial position, door opening angle, and hinge side, the policy autonomously completes the entire sequence from approach and stabilization to push-through.
overview:
Humanoid loco-manipulation—performing physical tasks while walking—is notoriously hard because it requires tight synchronization between bipedal dynamic balance and hand contact forces. Prior works often relied on tracking predefined reference motions, routing through coarse intermediate interfaces like velocity commands, or splitting control between separate upper- and lower-body controllers. However, these choices limit adaptive responses to unforeseen situations.

To tackle this, the authors propose "ViLoMan," a framework that synthesizes physically plausible whole-body trajectories in simulation from human contact data, then uses them to train a unified policy driven solely by onboard sensors. First, human door-interaction data is smoothly connected with approaching walks generated by a generative motion model, then refined via physics-based tracking and door diversification to form an executable dataset. Next, a privileged teacher policy is trained with reinforcement learning using full state information. Finally, online DAgger distills this teacher into a single student neural network taking only egocentric depth frames and proprioceptive measurements as input.

Experiments were conducted on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid across varied door geometries and initial poses. ViLoMan achieved a 77.55% success rate in simulation and an 80% success rate on the real Unitree G1 hardware, validating the power of direct joint-level control without intermediate commands or reference trajectories.
contributions: Built an automated pipeline that synthesizes approaching walks onto human contact data and enforces physical plausibility to create diverse, executable humanoid loco-manipulation trajectories.

Designed a residual teacher policy built on a general whole-body tracker to handle privileged contact dynamics, together with an online DAgger distillation strategy to transfer it to onboard sensory inputs.

Demonstrated unified end-to-end control that directly outputs 29 joint target positions at 50Hz relying only on a head-mounted depth camera and proprioception, without reference motions or intermediate task-space commands.
Achieved zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer on a physical Unitree G1 with an 80% success rate across diverse initial setups for approach, contact, and door closing.

sections.heading: Why is humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation so hard?
sections.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation faces two primary bottlenecks: a lack of physically executable contact interaction data and the difficulty of unified whole-body coordination from onboard sensors alone. While previous approaches relied on decoupled controllers or intermediate interfaces, this paper achieves fully autonomous direct joint control via data synthesis and privileged teacher-student distillation.
sections.details:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires a robot to traverse its workspace while physically interacting with objects. It is exceptionally demanding because the robot must generate and absorb substantial contact forces at its end-effectors while preserving bipedal dynamic balance.

Two core challenges lie at the heart of this problem:
- First is the data collection bottleneck. Collecting teleoperation or reinforcement learning demonstrations on real hardware is prohibitively expensive. Meanwhile, abundant Human-Object Interaction (HOI) datasets exist, but morphological discrepancies cause them to violate joint limits and contact constraints when mapped directly onto robots. Furthermore, human datasets usually capture only the moment of pushing or pulling, lacking the preceding approach walk.
- Second is direct control from onboard sensors. Controlling high-DoF whole-body motions straight from camera images and joint telemetry yields an enormous search space. Existing approaches therefore tracked predefined reference motions, inserted task-space commands or discrete tokens as intermediate interfaces, or decoupled upper-body and lower-body controllers. Unfortunately, these designs reduce adaptability and break holistic whole-body coordination.

ViLoMan addresses both challenges head-on. It automatically splices generated approaching walks into human contact data, refines them into physically sound trajectories, trains a privileged teacher, and distills that teacher into an onboard-sensor student policy via online DAgger. This yields a truly autonomous whole-body coordination policy requiring neither reference motions nor intermediate representations at test time.

sections.heading: Prior work on human motion data and whole-body control
sections.summary: Prior efforts explored extracting robot skills from motion capture or video generation models, as well as whole-body control using task-space commands. However, gaps remained in synthesizing coherent long-horizon datasets and achieving unified visual control without intermediate representations.
sections.details:
Related work broadly divides into two lines: applying human motion data to robotics, and humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation.

Regarding human motion data, many 3D contact datasets utilize parametric body models like SMPL-X, and retargeting techniques have been developed to map these motions onto robot kinematics. Recent approaches extract contact relationships from video or generate robot motions using video generative models (such as GRAIL or Imagine2Real). Even so, automatically generating datasets that consistently cover the entire timeline from walking approach to contact manipulation while obeying robot dynamics remained challenging.

Regarding whole-body coordination, imitation learning tracking predefined references and hierarchical architectures bridging high-level planners to low-level controllers via end-effector velocities or sparse keypoints have been widely studied. While recent works incorporate onboard RGB or depth cameras for closed-loop control, most explicitly decouple locomotion from manipulation or still require reference motions at deployment.

ViLoMan stands out by eliminating dependence on intermediate representations and resolving physical inconsistencies over long horizons, completing the entire chain—from approach to contact and push-through—using direct joint-level control within a single neural network.

sections.heading: ViLoMan's architecture: from data augmentation to distillation
sections.summary: ViLoMan consists of three stages: physically plausible dataset generation, privileged residual teacher policy training, and online DAgger distillation to a student policy driven purely by onboard sensors. This enables reference-free, vision- and proprioception-based direct joint control at 50Hz.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation and Overview
The control target is the 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid running at 50Hz. During deployment, the student policy $\pi_{\mathrm{Student}}$ takes an 808-dimensional proprioceptive history $s_t^{\mathrm{prop}}$ (past angular velocities, gravity projection, joint positions/velocities, and previous actions) along with 4 frames of egocentric depth images $I_{t-3:t}^{\mathrm{depth}}$ ($4 \times 36 \times 64$) to directly output 29-dimensional target joint positions $a_t^{\mathrm{student}}$.

### III-B Constructing Physically Executable Motion Data
To build high-quality training trajectories from human motion, the data passes through the following pipeline:
- **Contact-Preserving Retargeting**: Door-closing motions are extracted from the TRUMANS dataset and retargeted to G1 kinematics via OmniRetarget while preserving geometric contact relationships between hands and doors.
- **Approach Walk Synthesis via Generative Model**: Because human clips begin right in front of the door, Kimodo, a motion generation model compatible with G1, synthesizes approach trajectories from various initial positions toward the pre-contact pose, smoothly stitching them together (producing 710 trajectories from 71 raw motions).
- **Door Diversification**: Parametric assets from DoorGym are leveraged to randomize handle geometry (lever, round knob, pull handle), hinge side (left/right), door dimensions, and opening angles.
- **Physical Refinement and Filtering**: Splicing motions purely geometrically causes the robot to fall over. A reinforcement learning policy tracks both the robot and the door in simulation to refine kinematics into physically valid trajectories. Dropping broken motions leaves 409 training and 106 test trajectories.

### III-C Privileged Teacher Policy Tracking Reference Motions
A pretrained general whole-body tracker (GMT from GentleHumanoid) serves as a frozen base. On top of it, a residual policy $\pi_{\mathrm{Res}}$ is added, observing privileged environmental states $c_t^{\mathrm{int}}$ such as object state and contact targets. By letting the base model handle basic walking balance while the residual policy learns contact force adjustments via PPO as $\Delta a_t^{\mathrm{res}}$, the system achieves stable training alongside high contact performance.

### III-D Distillation to Visual-Proprioceptive Student Policy
Because the privileged teacher requires ground-truth environment states and future reference trajectories, it cannot run directly on the real robot. ViLoMan distills this capability into a student policy combining a small CNN for depth features (32 dimensions) and an MLP for joint outputs. Plain offline behavioral cloning (BC) suffers from covariate shift caused by compounding errors. Instead, the authors apply online DAgger, where the teacher labels states actually visited by the student. This yields a robust closed-loop policy that responds directly to depth changes without any reference motion.

sections.heading: Experimental validation in simulation and on the real G1
sections.summary: In simulation, ViLoMan achieved a 77.55% success rate, significantly outperforming behavioral cloning and intermediate-representation baselines. Deployed on the physical Unitree G1 using only onboard depth sensing and proprioception, it completed unfamiliar door-closing tasks with an 80% success rate (32/40 trials).
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup and Metrics
Evaluations were conducted in the GPU-accelerated simulator "mjlab" (16,384 parallel environments) and on a physical Unitree G1. The test set comprises 106 unseen trajectories sourced from different original human motions than the training set. Metrics include "Survival Rate" (avoiding falls) and "Door-Closing SR" (closing the door to an angle under 10 degrees).

### IV-B Effect of Privileged Teacher and Online Distillation (Q1)
Ablation studies (Table II) highlight the role of each component:
- Directly deploying the pretrained tracker zero-shot yielded only a 4.53% success rate, whereas adding residual adaptation pushed the teacher to 84.91% success and 98.11% survival.
- In student distillation, offline behavioral cloning (BC) dropped to a 31.89% success rate due to compounding errors. Online DAgger boosted success to 77.55%, a 45.66-percentage-point gain.
- Removing depth input drastically reduced success, confirming that proprioception alone cannot resolve relative door positioning.

### IV-C Comparison of Execution Interfaces (Q2)
Comparisons against baselines using intermediate representations (Table III) demonstrate the benefits of direct joint control:
- SONIC, which operates via latent-space tokens, achieved high survival but managed only a 58.30% success rate, trailing ViLoMan by roughly 19 percentage points.
- Handoff, which uses a VLM (Qwen3-VL) to output 1Hz task-space commands like end-effector targets and base velocities, struggled with 16.79% to 20.94% success rates. Due to VLM inference latency, its execution took nearly twice as long as ViLoMan. Direct joint control proved far superior for agile whole-body coordination during contact.

### IV-D Real-World Transfer and Failure Analysis (Q3)
Deployed on a physical Unitree G1 using solely its head RealSense D435i depth camera and internal sensors, ViLoMan completed 32 out of 40 trials (80.0%) across 8 distinct initial configurations and door angles. This substantially outperformed the pure BC baseline (37.5%). Average execution time was just 6.6 seconds.

Failure analysis (Fig. F7) revealed that in missed attempts, the robot correctly approached and pushed the door, but stopped right before the 10-degree threshold because the narrowing gap between door and frame degraded visual depth contrast.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: ViLoMan generates physically coherent trajectories from incomplete human data and uses teacher-student distillation to achieve a unified humanoid whole-body policy driven purely by onboard sensors. Its effectiveness across simulation and real hardware opens new directions for autonomous loco-manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper presented ViLoMan, a scalable framework for learning whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation.

By augmenting human interaction data with synthesized approach walks and refining them through physics simulation, the authors eliminated the need for expensive real-world data collection. Furthermore, by distilling a privileged residual teacher into an onboard-sensor student policy via online DAgger, ViLoMan attains a unified direct joint-level control policy that requires no reference motions or high-level intermediate commands at test time.

Evaluated on articulated door closing, the policy exhibited solid generalization in simulation and strong zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer onto the physical Unitree G1. Combining geometric insights from human motion, physics-based policy training, and visual-proprioceptive integration offers a compelling blueprint for humanoids executing contact-rich physical tasks in real environments.

takeaways: Raw human contact data cannot be used directly, but combining generative motion models for approaching walks with physics-based tracking yields high-quality training trajectories.

For whole-body loco-manipulation, direct joint-level control from a single network outperforms intermediate interfaces like VLM task-space commands or latent tokens in both responsiveness and task success during contact.
When distilling privileged teacher knowledge into an onboard-sensor student, plain behavioral cloning collapses under covariate shift, making online DAgger on student-visited states essential.
limitations: Evaluation is confined to door-closing tasks, leaving generalizability to tensile-contact bimanual tasks (like pulling) or complex multi-stage manipulation unverified.
In blind spots where depth resolution or contrast drops—such as right before a door closes flush against the frame—contact judgments can falter, halting the motion just short of complete closure.

The pipeline relies heavily on external modules like Kimodo for approach generation and GentleHumanoid's GMT for the teacher base, resulting in notable overall training overhead and engineering complexity.
